text: What is the **contrapositive** of “if it rains, then the match is cancelled”?

options.t: If the match is cancelled, then it rains.
If it does not rain, then the match is not cancelled.
If the match is not cancelled, then it does not rain.
It rains and the match is not cancelled.

solution: Write the statement as $r \to c$ with $r$: it rains, $c$: the match is cancelled.
The contrapositive swaps the two sides **and** negates both: $\neg c \to \neg r$.
In words: if the match is not cancelled, then it does not rain. It is equivalent to the original.
concept: Contrapositive = swap and negate; it is the only variant equivalent to the original.

common_wrong.why: That only swaps the sides: it is the **converse** $c \to r$.
That only negates the sides: it is the **inverse** $\neg r \to \neg c$.
$r \wedge \neg c$ is the **negation** of the statement, the one situation it forbids.

text: On how many of the 8 rows of its truth table is $(p \vee q) \to r$ **false**?
solution: An implication is false exactly when its hypothesis is true and its conclusion false.
So we need $p \vee q$ = T and $r$ = F.
$p \vee q$ is true for 3 of the 4 settings of $(p, q)$ (all but FF), and $r$ must be F: $3 \times 1 = 3$ rows.
concept: Count the false rows of an implication as (rows with a true hypothesis) × (rows with a false conclusion).

common_wrong.why: Counting only the row $p = q = $ T: $p \vee q$ is inclusive, so TF and FT also make it true.
5 is the number of rows where the implication is **true** ($8 - 3$); the question asks for the false rows.

text: Let $e$: “you can enrol” and $f$: “you have paid the fee”. Which formula represents “you can enrol **only if** you have paid the fee”?
solution: “$p$ only if $q$” is $p \to q$: $p$ cannot happen without $q$.
Here $p = e$ and $q = f$, so the sentence is $e \to f$.
Check by the forbidden situation: the sentence forbids enrolling without having paid, $e \wedge \neg f$, which is exactly the false row of $e \to f$.
concept: “p only if q” is p → q; the condition after “only if” is the conclusion.

common_wrong.why: $f \to e$ is “you can enrol **if** you have paid”, the converse.
$\neg e \to \neg f$ is the inverse of the sentence, equivalent to $f \to e$, the converse again.
The sentence promises nothing in the other direction: paying need not let you enrol.

text: Which of the following are logically equivalent to $p \to q$?
solution: $p \to q$ is false on exactly one row: $p$ = T, $q$ = F. A formula is equivalent to it iff it is false on that row and true on the other three.
(A) $\neg p \vee q$ is false only when $p$ = T and $q$ = F. Equivalent.

(B) The contrapositive $
eg q 	o 
eg p$ is false only when $
eg q$ = T, $
eg p$ = F, i.e. the same row. Equivalent.
(C) $q \to p$ is false at $q$ = T, $p$ = F, a different row. Not equivalent.

(D) $
eg(p \wedge 
eg q)$ is false exactly when $p \wedge 
eg q$ is true: the same row. Equivalent.
concept: Equivalent formulas have the same false rows; p → q ≡ ¬p ∨ q ≡ ¬q → ¬p ≡ ¬(p ∧ ¬q).

common_wrong.why: The converse $q \to p$ is a different claim: it fails on $p$ = F, $q$ = T where $p \to q$ holds.

$
eg(p \wedge 
eg q)$ is just $
eg p \vee q$ by De Morgan.

text: Which formula represents “$q$ unless $p$”?
solution: “Unless” means “if not”: “$q$ unless $p$” is “if not $p$, then $q$”.
So the formula is $\neg p \to q$, which is equivalent to $p \vee q$.
It forbids only the situation where $p$ fails and $q$ fails too.
concept: “q unless p” = ¬p → q = p ∨ q.

common_wrong.why:
$p 	o q$ forbids $p \wedge 
eg q$; the sentence forbids $
eg p \wedge 
eg q$.
$\neg q \to \neg p$ is the contrapositive of $p \to q$, so it is wrong for the same reason.
$q \to \neg p$ reads “$q$ only if not $p$”, a different claim.

text: On how many of the 8 assignments to $p, q, r$ do $p \to (q \to r)$ and $(p \to q) \to r$ take **different** truth values?
solution: $p \to (q \to r)$ is false only when $p$ = T, $q$ = T, $r$ = F (one row).
$(p \to q) \to r$ is false when $p \to q$ is T and $r$ is F: $(p, q) \in \{$TT, FT, FF$\}$ with $r$ = F (three rows).
They differ on the rows where exactly one is false: FTF and FFF.
So they differ on **2** rows; implication is not associative.
concept: → is right-associative and not associative; compare the false rows of the two groupings.

common_wrong.why: Treating → as associative. On $p = q = r = $ F the first is T (false hypothesis) and the second is F.
That is the number of false rows of $(p \to q) \to r$; one of them (TTF) is also false for the other grouping.

text: The operator $\ast$ is defined by: $p \ast q$ is F when $p$ = T and $q$ = T, and T otherwise. Which formula is equivalent to $p \vee q$?
solution:
$\ast$ is false only on TT, so $p \ast q \equiv 
eg(p \wedge q) \equiv 
eg p \vee 
eg q$ (NAND).

$x \ast x \equiv 
eg x$, so $p \ast p \equiv 
eg p$ and $q \ast q \equiv 
eg q$.

(A) $
eg p \ast 
eg q \equiv 
eg
eg p \vee 
eg
eg q \equiv p \vee q$.

(B) is NAND, (C) is $
eg(
eg(p \wedge q)) = p \wedge q$, (D) is $p \ast 
eg q \equiv 
eg p \vee q$.
concept: Rewrite an operator from its false row (here NAND), then substitute each option.

common_wrong.why: Negating a NAND gives AND, not OR.
$p \ast (q \ast q) = p \ast \neg q = \neg p \vee q$, which is $p \to q$.
$p \ast q$ is the NAND itself, false only on TT.

text: It is known that $p \to q$ is **false**. What is the truth value of $(q \to r) \wedge (r \vee \neg p)$?
solution: $p \to q$ is false only when $p$ = T and $q$ = F. Nothing is known about $r$.
$q \to r = $ F $\to r$ = T whatever $r$ is.
$r \vee \neg p = r \vee $ F $= r$.
So the formula equals $r$: true if $r$ is true, false otherwise. It cannot be determined.
concept: A false implication fixes both its parts (p = T, q = F); evaluate the rest and see what is still free.

common_wrong.why: $q \to r$ is indeed true, but the second conjunct is just $r$, which is unknown.
$q$ is already known to be F, so this would make the formula always false; in fact it depends on $r$.

text: Which of the following say the same thing as “$x$ being even is **necessary** for $x$ to be divisible by 4”?

options.t: If $x$ is divisible by 4, then $x$ is even.
$x$ is even only if $x$ is divisible by 4.
$x$ is divisible by 4 only if $x$ is even.
If $x$ is not even, then $x$ is not divisible by 4.

solution: “$a$ is necessary for $b$” is $b \to a$. With $a$: $x$ even, $b$: $x$ divisible by 4, the sentence is $b \to a$.
(A) is $b \to a$. Same.
(B) is $a \to b$ (“$a$ only if $b$”), the converse. Different.
(C) is $b \to a$. Same.
(D) is $\neg a \to \neg b$, the contrapositive of $b \to a$. Same.
concept: The necessary condition is the conclusion; “p only if q” and the contrapositive say the same.

common_wrong.why: (B) reverses the direction: being even does not force divisibility by 4 ($x = 6$).
(D) is the contrapositive of (A), so it is equivalent.

text: How many assignments of truth values to $p, q, r, s$ make **exactly two** of the four variables true **and** make $p \to q$ true?
solution: Exactly two true: choose the true pair, $\binom{4}{2} = 6$ assignments.
$p \to q$ is false only when $p$ = T and $q$ = F. Among the pairs, those containing $p$ but not $q$ are $\{p, r\}$ and $\{p, s\}$.
Remove them: $6 - 2 = 4$ assignments ($\{p, q\}, \{q, r\}, \{q, s\}, \{r, s\}$).
concept: Count by complement: all rows meeting the count condition minus those on the implication's false row.

common_wrong.why: Forgetting the second condition: two of the pairs put $p$ = T, $q$ = F.
Removing $\{p, q\}$ as well: there $p \to q$ = T → T = T, so it stays.

text: Which one of the following formulas is a **contingency** (neither a tautology nor a contradiction)?
solution: (A): a conjunction implies each of its parts, so $(p \wedge q) \to p$ is a tautology (falsifying $p$ forces the hypothesis false).
(B): with $p$ = F, $q$ = T the hypothesis $p \to q$ is T and the conclusion F, so the formula is F; with $p$ = T it is T. Both values occur: a contingency.

(C): De Morgan gives $p \wedge 
eg p \wedge 
eg q$, a contradiction. (D): $p \vee 
eg p \vee 
eg q$, a tautology.
concept: A contingency needs one row that makes it true and one that makes it false; find both.

common_wrong.why: $(p \wedge q) \to p$ cannot be falsified: making $p$ false also makes the hypothesis false. It is a tautology.
$\neg(p \vee q)$ forces $p$ = F, which clashes with the first conjunct: a contradiction, not a contingency.

$
eg(p \wedge q) = 
eg p \vee 
eg q$ contains $
eg p$, so the whole disjunction is $p \vee 
eg p \vee \dots$, a tautology.

text: How many minterms appear in the principal disjunctive normal form of $p \to (q \wedge r)$ over the variables $p, q, r$?
solution: The PDNF has one minterm per row on which the formula is true.
If $p$ = F the implication is vacuously true: all 4 rows with $p$ = F count.
If $p$ = T we need $q \wedge r$: only the row TTT. Total $4 + 1 = 5$.
concept: The number of PDNF terms is the number of true rows; count the true rows of an implication by splitting on the hypothesis.

common_wrong.why: 3 is the number of **false** rows (maxterms): TTF, TFT, TFF.
Counting only the row where everything is true forgets the vacuously true rows with $p$ = F.

text: Variables are ordered $p, q, r$ with $p$ the most significant bit and T = 1. The formula $(p \vee q \vee \neg r) \wedge (\neg p \vee q \vee r)$ in maxterm notation is
solution: Both clauses contain every variable, so each is a maxterm; a maxterm is numbered by the single row that makes it **false**.
$p \vee q \vee \neg r$ is false when $p$ = 0, $q$ = 0, $r$ = 1: row 001 = 1.
$\neg p \vee q \vee r$ is false when $p$ = 1, $q$ = 0, $r$ = 0: row 100 = 4. So the formula is $\Pi(1, 4)$.
concept: Maxterm index = the falsifying row: plain literal → 0, negated literal → 1.

common_wrong.why: Numbering the clauses with the minterm rule (plain = 1) gives 110 = 6 and 011 = 3, the complementary rows.
Those are the true rows; they belong in $\Sigma(\dots)$, the PDNF, not in the PCNF.
Mixing both numbering rules double-counts each clause; a 2-clause PCNF has exactly 2 indices.

text: Which of the following are logically equivalent to $p \to (q \to r)$? (Select all that apply.)
solution: Rewrite the target: $p \to (q \to r) \equiv \neg p \vee \neg q \vee r$ (exportation).

(A) $
eg(p \wedge q) \vee r = 
eg p \vee 
eg q \vee r$: equal. (C) $
eg q \vee 
eg p \vee r$: equal (commutativity). (D) $
eg p \vee r \vee 
eg q \vee r$: equal (idempotence); this is hypothesis splitting.
(B) differs on $p = q = r =$ F: $(\text{T}) \to \text{F} = $ F, while the target is T.
concept: Exportation and hypothesis splitting: an ∧ in the hypothesis becomes an ∨ of implications.

common_wrong.why: → is not associative: $(p \to q) \to r$ is false on the all-false row, where $p \to (q \to r)$ is true.
(D) is also right: $(p \to r) \vee (q \to r) \equiv (p \wedge q) \to r$; the ∧ on the left turns into ∨.

text: Which one of the following sets of connectives is NOT functionally complete?
solution: All-T test: $\wedge$, $\vee$, $\to$ and $\leftrightarrow$ all give T when every input is T.
So every formula built from set D is T on the all-T row, and $\neg p$ (F when $p$ = T) cannot be built.

A, B and C are on the standard list: $p \wedge q \equiv 
eg(
eg p \vee 
eg q)$; $
eg p \equiv p 	o 	ext{F}$; $
eg p \equiv p \downarrow p$.
concept: A set whose connectives all preserve T (Post's class T₁) cannot build ¬.

common_wrong.why: With F available, $p \to \text{F} \equiv \neg p$, and $\neg p \to q \equiv p \vee q$: complete.
NOR alone builds $\neg p = p \downarrow p$ and $p \vee q = (p \downarrow q) \downarrow (p \downarrow q)$: complete.
De Morgan rebuilds ∧ from ¬ and ∨, and {¬, ∧, ∨} writes every PDNF.

text:
A Boolean function $f(x, y, z)$ is **self-dual** if $f(
eg x, 
eg y, 
eg z) = 
eg f(x, y, z)$ for every assignment. How many self-dual functions of three variables are there?
solution: The 8 rows pair up as (row, complemented row): 4 pairs.
Choosing $f$ on one row of a pair fixes it on the other ($f(\bar x) = \neg f(x)$), so each pair gives 2 choices.
concept: Self-dual functions of n variables: 2^(2^(n−1)).

common_wrong.why: 256 = $2^{2^3}$ counts all functions of three variables, not the self-dual ones.
70 = $\binom{8}{4}$ counts the neutral functions (four T rows), a different property.

text: The absorption law $p \vee (p \wedge q) \equiv p$ holds. By the duality principle, which of the following also holds?
solution: The dual swaps ∧ with ∨ (and T with F); variables and ¬ signs stay as they are.
The dual of $p \vee (p \wedge q)$ is $p \wedge (p \vee q)$, and the dual of $p$ is $p$.
Duality preserves equivalence, so $p \wedge (p \vee q) \equiv p$ (the other absorption law).
concept: Duality: swap ∧/∨ and T/F on both sides of an equivalence; do not negate the variables.

common_wrong.why: Duality does not negate the right-hand side; the dual of $p$ is $p$.
That is a substitution instance ($p \mapsto \neg p$, $q \mapsto \neg q$), true but not the dual: the connectives are unchanged.
Only one connective was changed; $p \vee (p \vee q) \equiv p \vee q$, not $p$.

text: Consider $S = ((p \to q) \to p) \to p$. Which one of the following is correct?
solution: Try to falsify: the conclusion $p$ must be F and the hypothesis $(p \to q) \to p$ must be T.
With $p$ = F, $p \to q$ = T, so the hypothesis is $\text{T} \to \text{F}$ = F. Clash.
No falsifying row exists: $S$ is a tautology (it is known as Peirce's law).
concept: Falsification: assume the formula is F, force values, and look for a clash.

common_wrong.why: A contingency needs a falsifying row; the forced values clash, so there is none.
'Satisfiable but not valid' is the same as contingency; $S$ is valid.
On $p$ = T the formula is $\dots \to \text{T}$ = T, so it is certainly satisfiable.

text: A CNF formula over the variables $p, q, r$ consists of **7 distinct clauses**, each containing all three variables exactly once (each literal plain or negated). How many truth assignments satisfy it?
solution: Each clause containing all three variables is a maxterm and is false on exactly one row.
Distinct maxterms are false on distinct rows, so the 7 clauses forbid 7 different rows.
Of the $2^3 = 8$ rows, $8 - 7 = 1$ survives.
concept: A full clause forbids one row; m distinct maxterms leave 2ⁿ − m satisfying rows.

common_wrong.why: 7 clauses cannot cover all 8 rows; you need all 8 maxterms for a contradiction.
7 is the number of forbidden rows, not the survivors.

text: Which of the following are tautologies? (Select all that apply.)
solution: (A) Falsify: $q$ = F, then the hypothesis needs $p$ = T and $p \to q$ = T, forcing $q$ = T. Clash: tautology (modus ponens).
(B) $q$ = T, $p$ = F: hypothesis T, conclusion F. Not a tautology (affirming the consequent).

(C) $
eg p \vee q \vee 
eg q \vee p$ contains $q \vee 
eg q$: tautology. (D) On $p$ = F the left side is F and the right side is $	ext{F} 	o 	ext{F}$ = T: not a tautology (∧ does not distribute over →).
concept: Falsify each option; one clean row refutes a tautology.

common_wrong.why: (D) claims ∧ distributes over →; the row $p$ = F breaks it.
(B) infers $p$ from $q$ and $p \to q$: the row $p$ = F, $q$ = T falsifies it.

text: Over the variables $p, q$ (with $p$ the most significant bit and T = 1), a formula has PDNF $\Sigma(0, 3)$. The formula is equivalent to
solution: Minterm 0 is row 00 ($p = q =$ F) and minterm 3 is row 11 ($p = q =$ T).
So the formula is $(\neg p \wedge \neg q) \vee (p \wedge q)$: true exactly when $p$ and $q$ agree.
That is $p \leftrightarrow q$.
concept: Read a Σ list as the rows where the formula is true.

common_wrong.why: $p \oplus q$ is $\Sigma(1, 2)$, the complementary rows.
That is only minterm 0; the row 11 is also true.
$p \to q$ is $\Sigma(0, 1, 3)$: it is also true on row 01.

text: Of the 16 Boolean functions of two variables, how many are functionally complete **on their own** (that is, the one-element set containing that function is functionally complete)?
solution: The function must escape $T_0$ and $T_1$: $f(\text{F}, \text{F}) = $ T and $f(\text{T}, \text{T}) = $ F. That leaves the two rows TF, FT free: 4 candidates.
Two of them are $\neg p$ and $\neg q$, which are self-dual (and affine), so they are trapped.
The other two are NAND and NOR, both complete. Answer 2.
concept: Post's criterion applied to a single connective: only NAND and NOR survive.

common_wrong.why: ¬p and ¬q pass the T₀/T₁ tests but are self-dual and affine; a function of one input cannot build ∧.
Most binary functions fail the all-T or all-F test (for example ∧ and ∨ preserve both).

text: From the premises $p \to q$ and $\neg q$ we conclude $\neg p$. Which rule of inference is this?
solution: The premise $\neg q$ denies the **conclusion** of the implication $p \to q$.
Going backwards from a denied conclusion to a denied hypothesis is modus tollens: $(\neg q \wedge (p \to q)) \to \neg p$ is a tautology.
Check: the only row with both premises true is $p = q = $ F, where $\neg p$ is true.
concept: Modus tollens: from p → q and ¬q, infer ¬p.

common_wrong.why: Modus ponens needs $p$ as a premise and concludes $q$; here we start from $\neg q$.
Disjunctive syllogism needs a disjunction $p \vee q$; although $p \to q \equiv \neg p \vee q$ makes the two related, the rule named for this shape is modus tollens.
Hypothetical syllogism chains two implications and concludes an implication, not a negation.

text: For the argument $p \vee q,\ \neg p \vee r \;\therefore\; q \vee r$, how many of the 8 rows of the truth table over $p, q, r$ are **critical rows** (rows on which every premise is true)?
solution: Split on $p$. If $p$ = T, the first premise is true and $\neg p \vee r$ needs $r$ = T; $q$ is free: 2 rows.
If $p$ = F, the second premise is true and $p \vee q$ needs $q$ = T; $r$ is free: 2 rows.
Total $2 + 2 = 4$ critical rows; on each one $q \vee r$ is true, so the resolution rule is valid.
concept: Critical rows are the rows where all premises hold; validity is checked only there.

common_wrong.why: 6 is the number of rows where $q \vee r$ (the conclusion) is true, not where both premises are.
Counting only one value of the free letter in each case; in each case one variable is unconstrained, giving 2 rows.

text: Which of the following arguments are **valid**?
solution: A is denying the antecedent: $p = $ F, $q = $ T makes both premises true and $\neg q$ false. Invalid.
B is hypothetical syllogism and D is disjunctive syllogism: both valid.
C treats $\vee$ as exclusive: $p = q = $ T makes both premises true and $\neg q$ false. Invalid.
concept: Find a counterexample row (premises T, conclusion F) to reject an argument; the standard rules have none.

common_wrong.why: A is the fallacy of denying the antecedent: the row $p$ = F, $q$ = T refutes it.
Logical $\vee$ is inclusive, so knowing $p$ tells you nothing about $q$.

text: Premises: “If it snows, the school closes.” “The school did not close.” Which conclusion follows by a valid rule?

options.t: If it does not snow, the school closes.
Nothing can be concluded about the snow.

solution: Let $s$: it snows, $c$: the school closes. Premises $s \to c$ and $\neg c$.
Modus tollens gives $\neg s$.
Check: the only critical row is $s = c = $ F, where $\neg s$ is true.
concept: Modus tollens: a denied conclusion denies the hypothesis.

common_wrong.why: This would be right for the premise “the school closed” (affirming the consequent gives nothing), but a **denied** consequent does give $\neg s$.

That is $
eg s 	o c$. We already know $
eg s$ (by modus tollens), so it would force $c$, contradicting the premise $
eg c$: it is false on the only critical row.
$s$ is false on the only critical row.

text: On how many of the 8 assignments to $p, q, r$ are **all three** of $p \to q$, $q \to r$, $r \to p$ true?
solution: The three implications form a cycle $p \to q \to r \to p$, so by hypothetical syllogism each letter implies every other.
So $p, q, r$ must all have the same value: if any one is T, all are T.
Exactly two assignments: TTT and FFF. The set is consistent (2 > 0).
concept: A cycle of implications forces all its letters to be equal.

common_wrong.why: Forgetting the all-false row: F → F is true, so FFF satisfies every implication.
Checking only two of the three implications; the third closes the cycle.

text:
Consider the clause set $\{p \vee q,\ 
eg p \vee q,\ p \vee 
eg q,\ 
eg p \vee 
eg q\}$. Which statement is correct?

options.t: It is satisfied by $p = q = $ T.
It is satisfiable, but resolution cannot derive the empty clause from it.
Resolution cannot be applied, because every pair of clauses clashes on two letters.
It is unsatisfiable, and the empty clause is derived in three resolution steps.

solution: Resolve $p \vee q$ with $\neg p \vee q$ on $p$: $q$.

Resolve $p \vee 
eg q$ with $
eg p \vee 
eg q$ on $p$: $
eg q$.
Resolve $q$ with $\neg q$: $\square$. Three steps; the set is unsatisfiable (each clause forbids one of the four rows).
concept: Each two-literal clause over p, q forbids one row; all four rows forbidden means unsatisfiable, and resolution finds □.

common_wrong.why: $p = q = $ T makes $\neg p \vee \neg q$ false.
$p \vee q$ and $\neg p \vee q$ clash only on $p$; only some pairs clash twice.
By refutation completeness, an unsatisfiable set always yields $\square$, and this set is unsatisfiable.

text: On an island of truth-tellers and liars, $A$ says: “We are both liars” (meaning $A$ and $B$). What are $A$ and $B$?

options.t: $A$ is a liar and $B$ is a truth-teller
$A$ is a truth-teller and $B$ is a liar

solution: Constraint: $a \leftrightarrow (\neg a \wedge \neg b)$.
If $a$ = T the statement would have to be true, but it says $A$ is a liar: impossible. So $a$ = F.

A liar's statement is false: $
eg(
eg a \wedge 
eg b)$ with $
eg a$ true needs $
eg b$ false, so $b$ = T.
concept: Speaker X saying S gives x ↔ S; a liar's statement must be false.

common_wrong.why: If both were liars, A's statement would be **true**, which a liar cannot say.
A truth-teller cannot call himself a liar.
Then the statement “we are both liars” would be false, but a truth-teller says only true things.

text: Let $S = \{p \to q,\ q \to r,\ r \to \neg p\}$. Which statements are true?
solution:
Chaining gives $p 	o 
eg p$, which is equivalent to $
eg p$: so $S \models 
eg p$ (B), and adding $p$ makes it inconsistent (D).
$S$ is consistent: $p = q = r = $ F satisfies all three (A).
C fails: $p = $ F, $q = $ F, $r = $ T satisfies $S$ (F → F, F → T, T → T) with $r$ true.
concept: Γ ⊨ C iff Γ ∪ {¬C} is inconsistent; a chain p → … → ¬p forces ¬p.

common_wrong.why: Forcing $\neg p$ does not make $S$ inconsistent: $p$ = F leaves room for models.
$r$ is not forced: with $p$ false, $r \to \neg p$ holds whatever $r$ is.

text: A theory over the variables $p, q$ has the single axiom $p \leftrightarrow q$ (with a sound and complete proof system). Which is true?

options.t: It is consistent but not complete: it proves neither $p$ nor $\neg p$.

solution: Models of $p \leftrightarrow q$: TT and FF. At least one model, so consistent.
$p$ is T on TT and F on FF: neither $p$ nor $\neg p$ holds in every model, so neither is provable.
A consistent theory with two models is not negation-complete.
concept: A consistent propositional theory is complete exactly when it has one model.

common_wrong.why: It decides some formulas (for example $p \to q$) but not $p$; completeness needs every formula decided.
The model FF makes $p$ false, so $p$ is not a consequence.
Two models exist, so no contradiction is derivable.

text: How many of the following are logical consequences of $\{p \vee q,\ \neg p\}$: $q$, $p$, $q \vee r$, $p \to r$, $\neg q$?
solution: The premises force $p$ = F and (by disjunctive syllogism) $q$ = T; $r$ is free.
$q$: yes. $q \vee r$: yes (addition). $p \to r$: yes, its hypothesis is false.
$p$ and $\neg q$: no. Count 3.
concept: With p forced false, anything of the form p → … follows vacuously.

common_wrong.why: Missing $p \to r$: an implication with a false hypothesis is true on every critical row.
Missing addition: $q \models q \vee r$ whatever $r$ is.

text: “If the password is correct, access is granted. Access was granted. So the password was correct.” This inference is
solution: Let $c$: password correct, $g$: access granted. Premises $c \to g$, $g$; conclusion $c$.
Reasoning backwards from a true conclusion is affirming the consequent.
Counterexample: $c$ = F, $g$ = T (access granted another way, say by an administrator).
concept: From p → q and q nothing follows about p.

common_wrong.why: Modus ponens would need the premise $c$ and conclude $g$; here it is the other way round.
Denying the antecedent starts from $\neg c$; this argument starts from $g$.
Modus tollens needs a **denied** consequent $\neg g$.
